track.title: People Skills at Work
track.tagline: Practise corporate communication and people skills every day

lessons.title: Technical skill gets you in; people skills move you up
lessons.summary: Why relationships decide promotions as much as output.

sections.b: You do excellent work, but colleagues with weaker skills get noticed, promoted or chosen for projects. Often the difference is how they communicate, build relationships and make others' work easier.
They treat people skills as learnable skills, not personality. They practise small behaviours daily: greeting people, listening fully, sharing credit, updating proactively and asking good questions.

To yourself: 'Today I'll practise one people skill on purpose.'
To a colleague: 'How's your week going? Anything I can help with on the project?'
Believing 'my work should speak for itself'. Work speaks quietly; people need context, visibility and trust to value it.

speak: How's your week going?
Is there anything I can help with?
Thanks, that really helped me.
lessons.action: Pick one person you work with and have a 2-minute non-work chat with them today.

quiz.q: Why do people skills matter for promotions?
options: Others must trust and want to work with you

quiz.q: People skills are best seen as…
'My work will speak for itself' is risky because…
options: Work needs context and visibility to be valued

lessons.title: Know your communication style
lessons.summary: Understand how you come across before changing it.

sections.b: Technical people often come across as blunt, quiet or overly detailed, while they intend to be efficient or precise.
They ask for honest feedback on how they come across, notice patterns (e.g. interrupting, long explanations, rarely smiling) and adapt their style to the listener.

'Could I ask for quick feedback? When I explain things in meetings, is it clear, or too detailed?'
'If there's one thing I could do to communicate better with you, what would it be?'
Assuming people understand your intent. Others judge your behaviour, not your intentions.

speak: Could I ask for quick feedback on how I communicate?
Is my explanation clear, or too detailed?
What's one thing I could do better?
lessons.action: Ask one trusted colleague: 'What's one thing I could do to communicate better?' and just listen.

quiz.q: A common blind spot for technical experts is…
The fastest way to learn your style is…

lessons.title: First impressions in the office
lessons.summary: The first 30 seconds set the tone for a relationship.

sections.b: Meeting new colleagues, clients or leaders, you may freeze, avoid eye contact or jump straight into work.
They make eye contact, smile, use the person's name, introduce themselves with a one-line role description, and ask a friendly question.
'Hi Priya, I'm Yash from the finance team. I work on monthly reporting. Nice to finally meet you. How long have you been with the sales team?'
Looking at your phone, a weak mumbled introduction, or talking only about yourself.

speak: Hi, I'm Yash from the finance team.
Nice to finally meet you.
How long have you been with the team?
lessons.action: Introduce yourself to one person you haven't properly met, using your name, team and one-line role.

options: Name, team and a one-line role

lessons.title: Small talk that doesn't feel fake
lessons.summary: Short friendly chats build trust over time.

sections.b: You find small talk pointless or awkward, so you skip it and seem distant.
They see small talk as relationship-building. They ask open questions, remember details (kids, hobbies, trips) and follow up later.

'How was your weekend? Did you end up going to Jaipur?'
'That sounds fun. What was the best part?'
Later: 'How did your daughter's exam go?'
Yes/no questions only, talking about controversial topics, or one-word answers.

speak: How was your weekend?
What was the best part?
How did the trip go?
lessons.action: Start one small-talk conversation today and remember one detail to follow up on next week.

options: Remembering and asking about a detail later

quiz.q: Better question type for small talk is…

lessons.title: Active listening
lessons.summary: Make people feel heard, and understand them better.

sections.b: In discussions you're often preparing your answer instead of listening, or you interrupt to correct details.
They listen fully, nod, take notes, paraphrase key points and ask clarifying questions before responding.

'So if I understand correctly, the main concern is the deadline, not the budget?'
'Tell me more about that.'
'What would a good outcome look like for you?'
Interrupting, looking at your laptop, or jumping to solutions too quickly.

speak: So if I understand correctly, the main concern is the deadline?
Tell me more about that.
What would a good outcome look like for you?
lessons.action: In one conversation today, paraphrase what the other person said before giving your view.

quiz.q: A sign of poor listening is…

lessons.title: Managing your emotions at work
lessons.summary: Stay calm when you're frustrated or criticised.

sections.b: When your work is criticised or a colleague is unreasonable, you react sharply or shut down.
They pause before responding, name the emotion to themselves ('I'm frustrated'), ask questions to understand, and respond later if needed.

'That's a fair point. Let me think about it and come back to you by tomorrow.'
'Can you help me understand what concerns you most?'
Replying instantly to an annoying email, raising your voice, or sulking silently.

speak: That's a fair point. Let me think about it.
Can you help me understand your concern?
I'll come back to you by tomorrow.
lessons.action: Next time you feel irritated at work, wait 10 seconds and ask one question before responding.

quiz.q: A good first reaction to criticism is…
Replying to an annoying email immediately…

lessons.title: Body language and presence
lessons.summary: Your posture and face speak before you do.

sections.b: You may sit slouched, avoid eye contact or look serious, so people think you're uninterested or unapproachable.
They sit upright, face the speaker, nod, keep an open posture and smile naturally. On video calls they look at the camera and keep it on.
Non-verbal: lean slightly forward when listening; nod; brief eye contact; relaxed smile when greeting.
Crossed arms, checking your phone in meetings, or a blank face on camera.

speak: I'm glad to be part of this discussion.
That's interesting, please go on.
Thanks for explaining that.
lessons.action: In your next meeting, keep your phone away and maintain an open, attentive posture.

quiz.q: Checking your phone in meetings signals…

lessons.title: Remembering names and details
lessons.summary: A small habit with big relationship returns.

sections.b: You forget names of people from other teams, which feels awkward and distant.
They repeat the name when introduced, connect it to something memorable, and note key details after meetings (team, project, interests).

'Nice to meet you, Ankit. Ankit from procurement, right?'
If you forget: 'I'm sorry, remind me of your name again?' (honest is better than avoiding).
Avoiding people because you forgot their name.

speak: Nice to meet you, Ankit.
Ankit from procurement, right?
Sorry, could you remind me of your name?
lessons.action: Write down names and one detail of 3 people you interacted with this week.

quiz.q: A trick to remember names is…
If you forget a name, it's best to…

lessons.title: Being approachable
lessons.summary: People bring opportunities to those who seem open.

sections.b: Colleagues hesitate to ask you questions because you seem busy, serious or irritated.
They respond warmly to questions, say 'good question', share knowledge generously and signal availability ('Ping me anytime about the model').

'Good question. Happy to explain.'
'I'm in the middle of something; can we talk at 3?'
'Feel free to ping me anytime about this.'
Sighing, short replies or making people feel stupid for asking.

speak: Good question, happy to explain.
Can we talk at three? I'm finishing something.
Feel free to ping me anytime.
lessons.action: When someone asks you a question today, start with 'Good question' and explain kindly.

quiz.q: If busy, a good response is…
Making people feel stupid for asking…

lessons.title: Saying thank you specifically
lessons.summary: Specific appreciation is remembered.

sections.b: You say 'thanks' automatically or forget to recognise others' help.
They thank people specifically, mention the impact, and sometimes thank them in front of their manager or the team.

'Thanks for pulling the data so quickly, Neha. It helped us finish the report a day early.'
In a group mail: 'Special thanks to Rohan for fixing the reconciliation issue.'
Generic 'thanks' only, or taking credit for team effort.

speak: Thanks for pulling the data so quickly.
It helped us finish a day early.
Special thanks to Rohan for his help.
lessons.action: Send one specific thank-you message today mentioning the impact of someone's help.

quiz.q: Thanking someone in front of their manager…

lessons.title: Understand your manager's priorities
lessons.summary: Help your manager succeed and you succeed too.

sections.b: You work hard on tasks but don't know what your manager is measured on or worried about.
They ask about their manager's goals and pressures, and align their work to those priorities.

'What are your top priorities this quarter?'
'What's keeping you up at night on this project?'
'How can I make your job easier?'
Assuming your priorities match your manager's.

speak: What are your top priorities this quarter?
How can I make your job easier?
What does success look like for you?
lessons.action: Ask your manager: 'What are your top three priorities this quarter?'

quiz.q: Knowing your manager's priorities helps you…
options: Align your work to what matters
How can I make your job easier?

lessons.title: Weekly updates that build trust
lessons.summary: Your manager should never have to chase you.

sections.b: Your manager asks 'What's the status?' frequently, which signals they lack visibility.
They send short, regular updates: done, next, risks/blocked, without being asked.
'Quick update: Done: reconciliation for March. Next: variance commentary by Thursday. Risk: waiting for sales data, which may delay by a day.'
Long unstructured messages, or updates only when something goes wrong.

speak: Quick update on the project.
The main risk is the delayed sales data.
I'll have the draft ready by Thursday.
lessons.action: Send your manager a 3-line update today: done, next, risks.

lessons.title: No surprises: escalate early
lessons.summary: Bad news ages badly.

sections.b: You hope to fix a problem quietly, but the manager hears about it from others, damaging trust.
They escalate risks early with options, so the manager can help or prepare.
'Heads-up: the vendor may miss Friday's delivery. Option A: we partially deliver; option B: we push the deadline by 3 days. I recommend A. What do you think?'
Hiding problems, or bringing problems without any options.

speak: Just a heads-up about a possible delay.
There are two options we could consider.
I recommend the first option.
lessons.action: Identify one risk in your current work and inform your manager with two options.

options: They hear bad news from others first

lessons.title: Running a great 1:1
lessons.summary: Use 1:1s to grow, not just report status.

sections.b: Your 1:1s are short status updates or get cancelled.
They prepare an agenda: wins, blockers, decisions needed, feedback and career. They take notes and follow up.
'For today I have three things: a quick win, one decision I need from you, and I'd like your feedback on my presentation.'
Coming unprepared or only talking about tasks.

speak: I have three things for today.
There's one decision I need from you.
Could I get your feedback on my presentation?
lessons.action: Prepare a 3-point agenda for your next 1:1 with your manager.

lessons.title: Asking for help without seeming weak
lessons.summary: Smart people ask early and well.

sections.b: You stay stuck for days because you don't want to look incompetent.
They try first, then ask specific questions showing what they've tried.
'I've tried reconciling using the March ledger and the bank file, but there's a ₹2 lakh gap. Could you spare 10 minutes to look at it with me?'
Asking too early without effort, or too late after deadlines are at risk.

speak: I've tried two approaches already.
Could you spare ten minutes to look at this with me?
What would you suggest I try next?
lessons.action: If stuck on anything today, ask for help with a specific question and what you've tried.

options: What you've tried and a specific question

quiz.q: Waiting too long to ask for help can…
Asking good questions is seen as…

lessons.title: Disagreeing with your manager
lessons.summary: Respectful disagreement builds credibility.

sections.b: You disagree with your manager's decision but stay quiet or complain to peers.
They raise concerns privately, with data and alternatives, then commit if the decision stands ('disagree and commit').
'Can I share a concern about the timeline? Based on last quarter's data, testing took two weeks. Could we consider…? If we still go ahead, I'll fully support it.'
Arguing in front of others, or silently not following the decision.

speak: Can I share a concern about the timeline?
Based on last quarter's data, testing took two weeks.
If we still go ahead, I'll fully support it.
lessons.action: Practise phrasing one concern you have as: concern + data + alternative.

quiz.q: Where is it best to disagree with your manager?

options: Voice concerns, then support the decision

lessons.title: Understanding your manager's style
lessons.summary: Adapt to how your manager works.

sections.b: Your manager prefers short messages but you send long emails, or they like calls and you only email.
They observe and ask: preferred channel, level of detail, best time to talk, and how they like decisions presented.

'Do you prefer quick updates on chat, or a summary email at the end of the week?'
'Would you like the headline first or the full detail?'
Assuming one style fits all managers.

speak: Do you prefer updates on chat or email?
Would you like the headline first?
When is a good time to discuss this?
lessons.action: Ask your manager how they prefer updates and adjust this week.

options: Why do you work like that?

lessons.title: Asking for feedback regularly
lessons.summary: Don't wait for the annual review.

sections.b: You only learn what your manager thinks during appraisals, when it's too late to change.
They ask for specific feedback monthly and act on it visibly.

'What's one thing I did well this month and one thing I could improve?'
'Last time you suggested shorter updates; have you noticed a difference?'
Asking 'Any feedback?' (too vague) or arguing when receiving it.

speak: What's one thing I did well this month?
What's one thing I could improve?
Thank you, I'll work on that.
lessons.action: Ask your manager: 'What's one thing I could do better next month?'

options: What's one thing I could improve next month?

lessons.title: Making your achievements visible
lessons.summary: Help your manager advocate for you.

sections.b: Your manager doesn't remember your wins at appraisal time.
They keep a 'wins log' with numbers and share highlights regularly, framed as team impact.

'Quick win to share: the automated report went live and saves the team about 10 hours a week.'
At appraisal: 'Here are my top 5 contributions this year with impact.'
Bragging constantly, or never mentioning wins.

speak: Quick win to share with you.
The new report saves the team ten hours a week.
Here are my top contributions this year.
lessons.action: Start a 'wins log' today and add your last three achievements with numbers.

options: Regular and framed as team impact

lessons.title: Career conversations
lessons.summary: Tell your manager what you want next.

sections.b: You hope your manager will notice your ambitions, but they're focused on today's work.
They state goals clearly, ask what skills are needed, request stretch opportunities and review progress every few months.
'In the next 12-18 months I'd like to move toward an FP&A lead role. What skills or experiences would make me ready? Could I take ownership of the budget process this year?'
Expecting promotions without discussing them, or demanding them without a plan.

speak: In the next year I'd like to move toward a lead role.
What skills would make me ready?
Could I take ownership of the budget process?
lessons.action: Write your 12-month career goal and one stretch opportunity to request.

options: A challenging task that builds new skills

quiz.q: A good question to ask is…
options: Why am I not promoted yet?
What skills would make me ready?

lessons.title: Building relationships with peers
lessons.summary: Peers become your network, allies and future leaders.

sections.b: You interact with colleagues only when you need something from them.
They invest before they need: lunch or coffee chats, helping with small things, sharing useful info and celebrating others' wins.

'Want to grab a coffee this week? I'd love to understand how your team works.'
'Saw this article on automation, thought it might help your project.'
Transactional relationships: only reaching out when you need a favour.

speak: Want to grab a coffee this week?
I'd love to understand how your team works.
I saw this and thought of your project.
lessons.action: Invite one peer from another team for a 15-minute coffee or call this week.

lessons.title: Sharing credit generously
lessons.summary: Credit shared multiplies; credit hoarded divides.

sections.b: In presentations you say 'I did this' even though others contributed, and colleagues feel unappreciated.
They name contributors specifically and talk about 'we' for team work and 'I' only for their own part.
'This dashboard was a team effort. Rahul cleaned the data and Meera designed the visuals; I built the model.'
Taking credit for others' work or never mentioning helpers.

speak: This was a team effort.
Rahul cleaned the data and Meera designed the visuals.
I built the forecasting model.
lessons.action: In your next update or presentation, name at least one colleague's contribution.

options: 'We' for team and 'I' for your part

lessons.title: Helping without overcommitting
lessons.summary: Be generous, but protect your time.

sections.b: You say yes to every request and end up overloaded and late on your own work.
They help when possible, clarify scope and time, and say no kindly with alternatives when needed.

'I can help for 30 minutes this afternoon.'
'I'd like to help, but I'm on a deadline until Thursday. Could we look at it on Friday, or would Ankit be able to help sooner?'
Saying yes and then delivering late, or a blunt 'no'.

speak: I can help for thirty minutes this afternoon.
I'm on a deadline until Thursday.
Could we look at it on Friday?
lessons.action: Practise one 'kind no' with an alternative this week.

quiz.q: Saying yes to everything leads to…

options: Agreeing how much help and when

lessons.title: Working across departments
lessons.summary: Different teams, different priorities.

sections.b: Sales, operations and finance clash because each sees only its own goals.
They learn other teams' targets and pain points, speak their language and frame requests around shared goals.
'I know month-end is busy for you. To help both teams, could we agree on a 2-day cut-off for invoices? It'll reduce your follow-up calls too.'
Using your team's jargon, or blaming other departments.

speak: I know month-end is busy for you.
Could we agree on a two-day cut-off?
It'll reduce follow-up calls for both teams.
lessons.action: Ask someone from another department: 'What's your biggest challenge working with our team?'

quiz.q: To work well across departments, learn…

lessons.title: Asking colleagues for favours
lessons.summary: Make it easy for people to say yes.

sections.b: Your requests get ignored or delayed.
They make specific, polite requests with context, deadline and reason, and thank afterwards.
'Hi Neha, could you share the Q3 sales file by Wednesday 3 pm? I need it for the board deck on Thursday. Thanks so much!'
Vague requests ('send the data'), no deadline, or urgent requests at the last minute.

speak: Could you share the sales file by Wednesday?
I need it for the board deck on Thursday.
Thanks so much for your help!
lessons.action: Rewrite one request you need to make using: specific ask + deadline + reason.

quiz.q: After help is given you should…

lessons.title: Handling a difficult colleague
lessons.summary: Focus on behaviour, not personality.

sections.b: A colleague is rude, misses deadlines or dismisses your ideas.
They stay professional, talk privately about specific behaviours and impact, seek understanding, and escalate only after trying directly.
'Can we talk for a minute? In the last two meetings my points were interrupted. I'd like to make sure we both get heard. How can we handle this better?'
Complaining behind their back, matching their rudeness, or avoiding them entirely.

speak: Can we talk for a minute?
I'd like to make sure we both get heard.
How can we handle this better?
lessons.action: Write a private, calm opening line for a conversation with one challenging colleague.

quiz.q: With a difficult colleague, focus on…

lessons.title: Team trust: reliability
lessons.summary: Do what you say, when you say.

sections.b: Small missed commitments make colleagues stop relying on you.
They commit carefully, write down promises, deliver on time or warn early if they can't.

'I'll send it by 4 pm.' (and do it)
'Quick heads-up: I'll need until tomorrow 11 am instead of today; the data came late.'
Vague commitments ('I'll try') or silent delays.

speak: I'll send it by four o'clock.
Quick heads-up, I'll need until tomorrow morning.
Done, it's in your inbox.
lessons.action: List today's promises you've made and deliver or update on each.

options: Warn early with a new time

lessons.title: Celebrating others
lessons.summary: Recognising peers builds a positive culture.

sections.b: Team wins go unnoticed; birthdays and milestones pass without acknowledgement.
They congratulate peers publicly, remember milestones and share wins in team channels.

'Huge congratulations, Meera, on clearing the CFA Level 2! Well deserved.'
'Shout-out to the ops team for closing the audit early.'
Ignoring others' success or seeing it as competition.

speak: Huge congratulations, well deserved!
Shout-out to the ops team.
Great job on the presentation.
lessons.action: Post one genuine shout-out for a colleague in a team channel this week.

quiz.q: A good place for shout-outs is…

lessons.title: Collaborating on shared work
lessons.summary: Clear roles prevent duplicate work and blame.

sections.b: Projects stall because nobody knows who does what.
They clarify roles, owners and deadlines at the start, and use shared trackers.
'To avoid confusion, can we agree who owns each part? I'll take the model, Rahul the data, Meera the slides, by Friday.'
Assuming roles, or doing others' parts silently and then resenting it.

speak: Can we agree who owns each part?
I'll take the model.
Let's review progress on Friday.
lessons.action: For one shared task, write owner + deadline for each part and share it.

quiz.q: Silently doing others' work leads to…

lessons.title: Office gossip
lessons.summary: Stay out of it without being cold.

sections.b: Colleagues gossip about others or management, and you feel pressure to join.
They don't spread gossip, redirect the conversation politely, and avoid saying anything they wouldn't say to the person.

'I haven't heard about that. Anyway, how's your project going?'
'I'd rather not guess; maybe we can ask her directly.'
Joining in, sharing confidential information, or lecturing others harshly.

speak: I haven't heard about that.
Anyway, how's your project going?
Maybe we can ask her directly.
lessons.action: If gossip comes up today, redirect with a neutral question.

quiz.q: A safe way to handle gossip is…

options: Don't say what you wouldn't say to the person

lessons.title: Preparing for meetings
lessons.summary: Five minutes of prep makes you sound sharp.

sections.b: You join meetings without knowing the purpose and stay quiet or ramble.
They check the agenda, prepare 1-2 points or questions, and bring key numbers.

Before: 'What's the decision we need today?'
In meeting: 'I have one point on the budget and one question about the timeline.'
Joining blind, or reading emails during the meeting.

speak: I have one point on the budget.
And one question about the timeline.
What decision do we need today?
lessons.action: Before your next meeting, write one point and one question you'll contribute.

options: Knowing the purpose and preparing points
What's the decision we need today?

lessons.title: Speaking up in meetings
lessons.summary: Your ideas only count if you share them.

sections.b: You have good ideas but stay silent because others speak faster or you fear being wrong.
They speak within the first 10 minutes, keep points short, build on others' ideas and use bridging phrases.

'Building on Ravi's point, we could also…'
'Can I add something here?'
'One quick thought: …'
Waiting for the perfect moment, or long rambling contributions.

speak: Building on Ravi's point, we could also automate this.
Can I add something here?
One quick thought on the timeline.
lessons.action: Make one contribution in the first 10 minutes of your next meeting.

lessons.title: Interrupting politely
lessons.summary: Enter the conversation without being rude.

sections.b: Fast talkers dominate; you can't get a word in.
They use a polite interruption, signal with a raised hand on video, and keep it brief.

'Sorry to jump in, but…'
'If I may add one point…'
'Before we move on, could I share something?'
Talking over people, or giving up entirely.

speak: Sorry to jump in, but I have a quick point.
If I may add one thing.
Before we move on, could I share something?
lessons.action: Use 'Sorry to jump in, but…' once this week when you need the floor.

quiz.q: On video calls you can signal by…
options: Raising your hand (or using the hand icon)

lessons.title: When someone talks over you
lessons.summary: Hold your ground calmly.

sections.b: Colleagues interrupt you mid-sentence.
They calmly finish their point, or reclaim the floor after the interruption.

'I'd like to finish my point, then I'm keen to hear yours.'
'Coming back to what I was saying…'
Getting angry or giving up.

speak: I'd like to finish my point.
Then I'm keen to hear yours.
Coming back to what I was saying.
lessons.action: Practise 'I'd like to finish my point' aloud three times.

quiz.q: If interrupted, a calm response is…
'Coming back to what I was saying' helps…

lessons.title: Asking smart questions
lessons.summary: Good questions make you look thoughtful.

sections.b: You hesitate to ask questions, fearing they'll seem basic.
They ask clarifying and strategic questions that help the whole group.

'What's the main risk if we delay?'
'How will we measure success?'
'Just to clarify, are we optimising for cost or speed?'
Asking questions to show off, or never asking.

speak: How will we measure success?
What's the main risk if we delay?
Are we optimising for cost or speed?
lessons.action: Ask one clarifying question in your next meeting.

lessons.title: Summarising decisions and actions
lessons.summary: Be the person who brings clarity.

sections.b: Meetings end without clear decisions; nobody knows who does what.
They summarise at the end: decisions, owners, deadlines, and send a short recap.
'Let me quickly recap: we agreed on option B; Neha will update the forecast by Friday; I'll share the deck on Monday.'
Leaving without clarity or long, unstructured minutes.

speak: Let me quickly recap.
We agreed on option B.
Neha will update the forecast by Friday.
lessons.action: Offer to summarise actions at the end of your next meeting.

quiz.q: A short recap email is sent…

lessons.title: Presenting your work in meetings
lessons.summary: Lead with the answer, then the details.

sections.b: You explain your analysis step by step and lose the audience before reaching the conclusion.
They lead with the conclusion, give 2-3 reasons and offer details if asked.
'The bottom line: we're 5% over budget, mainly due to freight costs. I recommend renegotiating with two vendors. Happy to walk through the details.'
Starting with methodology, or too many slides.

speak: The bottom line is we're five percent over budget.
The main reason is freight costs.
I recommend renegotiating with two vendors.
lessons.action: Rewrite one update so the first sentence is the conclusion.

lessons.title: Handling tough questions in meetings
lessons.summary: Stay calm, honest and structured.

sections.b: A senior asks a hard question and you panic or guess.
They pause, clarify the question, answer what they know, and promise a follow-up for what they don't.
'Good question. If I understand correctly, you're asking about the Q4 impact. We expect about 3%; I'll confirm the exact number by tomorrow.'
Bluffing numbers, getting defensive, or long rambles.

speak: If I understand correctly, you're asking about Q4.
We expect about three percent.
I'll confirm the exact number by tomorrow.
lessons.action: Practise the line: 'I don't have that exact figure, but I'll get back to you by tomorrow.'

quiz.q: If you don't know an answer…
options: Say what you know and promise a follow-up

lessons.title: Running your own meeting
lessons.summary: Short, focused meetings earn respect.

sections.b: Your meetings run long and drift off-topic.
They send an agenda with the goal, invite only needed people, timebox topics and end with actions.

'The goal today is to agree on the vendor. We have 30 minutes: 10 for options, 15 for discussion, 5 for decision.'
'Let's park that and take it offline.'
No agenda, too many attendees, or ending without decisions.

speak: The goal today is to agree on the vendor.
We have thirty minutes.
Let's park that and take it offline.
lessons.action: For your next meeting, write a one-line goal and a timed agenda.

lessons.title: Virtual meeting presence
lessons.summary: Show up well on video calls.

sections.b: On calls you're on mute, camera off and invisible.
They turn the camera on for important calls, use good lighting, speak first in round-robins and use chat for links and summaries.

'Hi everyone, Yash here from finance.'
'I'll drop the link in the chat.'
'Could everyone see my screen?'
Multitasking visibly, background noise, or never speaking.

speak: Hi everyone, Yash here from finance.
I'll drop the link in the chat.
Can everyone see my screen?
lessons.action: In your next video call, turn your camera on and speak in the first five minutes.

quiz.q: For important calls, it's best to…
A good use of chat is…

lessons.title: Writing clear emails
lessons.summary: Make every email easy to read and act on.

sections.b: Your emails are long, and people miss the key ask or don't reply.
They write a clear subject, put the ask in the first two lines, use bullets and end with a deadline.

Subject: 'Approval needed: Q3 budget revision by Friday'
'Hi Ravi, could you approve the revised Q3 budget by Friday? Key changes: • Freight +₹12 L • Marketing −₹5 L. Details attached.'
Burying the ask at the end, vague subjects like 'Update', or walls of text.

speak: Could you approve the revised budget by Friday?
The key changes are listed below.
Details are attached.
lessons.action: Rewrite your next email so the ask is in the first two lines.

quiz.q: Where should the main ask go?

options: Approval needed: Q3 budget by Friday

lessons.title: Tone in written messages
lessons.summary: Text loses tone; choose words carefully.

sections.b: Short messages like 'Why is this late?' sound angry, even if you're just asking.
They add greeting, context and softeners, and reread messages from the receiver's point of view.
Instead of 'Why is this late?': 'Hi Neha, just checking on the report. Is anything blocking you? Happy to help.'
ALL CAPS, many exclamation marks, or one-word replies like 'Ok.'

speak: Hi Neha, just checking on the report.
Is anything blocking you?
Happy to help if needed.
lessons.action: Reread three messages before sending today and soften any that sound harsh.

quiz.q: A softer version of 'Why is this late?' is…

lessons.title: Chat etiquette (Teams, Slack, WhatsApp)
lessons.summary: Respect time and attention in chats.

sections.b: You send 'Hi' and wait, or message colleagues late at night expecting replies.
They write the full message at once, respect working hours, use threads and set clear urgency.

Instead of 'Hi' (wait): 'Hi Ankit, quick question: is the vendor invoice approved? Need it for today's payment run by 3 pm.'
Late night: schedule the message for the morning.
Sending 'Hi' alone, spamming group chats, or expecting instant replies at night.

speak: Quick question: is the vendor invoice approved?
I need it for today's payment run by three.
No rush, tomorrow morning is fine.
lessons.action: Send your next chat message as one complete message with the ask and timing.

quiz.q: Instead of sending just 'Hi', you should…
options: Send the full question at once

lessons.title: Following up without nagging
lessons.summary: Persistent and polite gets results.

sections.b: People don't reply, and you feel awkward reminding them.
They follow up with context, make it easy to respond, and escalate politely after a couple of tries.

'Hi Ravi, gently bumping this up. Could you confirm by Thursday so we can close the vendor payment?'
'Would a quick 5-minute call be easier?'
Angry reminders, or giving up silently.

speak: Gently bumping this up.
Could you confirm by Thursday?
Would a quick five-minute call be easier?
lessons.action: Follow up on one pending item today with a polite nudge and an easy option.

options: Context and an easy next step

quiz.q: Offering a short call helps when…

lessons.title: Writing for senior leaders
lessons.summary: Executives read the first lines only.

sections.b: Your updates to leadership are long and technical.
They lead with the conclusion, key numbers and decision needed, in under 100 words, with details attached.
'Summary: Q3 revenue is 4% below plan due to delayed client X orders. We expect recovery in Q4. Decision needed: approve ₹20 L marketing push by Oct 25.'
Technical jargon, long background, or no clear ask.

speak: Summary: revenue is four percent below plan.
We expect recovery in Q4.
Decision needed: approve the marketing push.
lessons.action: Write a 3-line executive summary of your current project.

quiz.q: A good length for an executive update is…

lessons.title: Saying no in writing
lessons.summary: Decline clearly but kindly.

sections.b: You avoid replying to requests you can't fulfil, leaving people waiting.
They reply promptly, say no clearly, give a short reason and offer an alternative.
'Thanks for thinking of me. I can't take this on this week because of the audit, but I could help after the 25th, or Meera may be able to help sooner.'
Ignoring the email, or overly long apologies.

speak: Thanks for thinking of me.
I can't take this on this week because of the audit.
I could help after the twenty-fifth.
lessons.action: Reply to one pending request you can't accept using reason + alternative.

options: Leaves people waiting and damages trust

quiz.q: Starting with 'Thanks for thinking of me' sounds…

lessons.title: Email escalations
lessons.summary: Escalate facts, not emotions.

sections.b: An issue isn't resolved and you're tempted to CC senior people angrily.
They escalate with a neutral summary: issue, impact, what's been tried, and what's needed, and inform the person first.
'Hi Ravi, as discussed, I'm looping in Priya to help unblock the vendor payment. Issue: invoice pending since Oct 5. Impact: supply delay risk. Needed: approval by Oct 21.'
Surprise CCs, emotional language or blame.

speak: I'm looping in Priya to help unblock this.
The invoice has been pending since October fifth.
We need approval by the twenty-first.
lessons.action: Draft a neutral escalation template: issue, impact, tried, needed.

options: Issue, impact, what's tried, what's needed

lessons.title: Meeting recaps and minutes
lessons.summary: Written recaps prevent confusion later.

sections.b: After meetings, people remember decisions differently.
They send a short recap within 24 hours with decisions, actions, owners and dates.
'Thanks all. Recap: • Decision: go with vendor B • Actions: Neha (contract by Oct 25), Yash (budget update by Oct 23). Let me know if I missed anything.'
No recap, or long transcripts nobody reads.

speak: Thanks all, here's a quick recap.
We decided to go with vendor B.
Let me know if I missed anything.
lessons.action: Send a 4-line recap after your next meeting.

quiz.q: 'Let me know if I missed anything' invites…

lessons.title: Writing persuasive proposals
lessons.summary: Get approvals with clear business cases.

sections.b: Your proposals are rejected or ignored.
They frame the problem, show the cost of inaction, propose a solution with numbers, address risks and give a clear ask.

'Problem: manual reconciliation takes 40 hours/month. Cost: ~₹2 L/month. Proposal: automation tool (₹5 L one-time), payback in 3 months. Risk: training time, mitigated by vendor support. Ask: approval by Nov 1.'
Focusing on features, not business impact.

speak: The problem is forty hours of manual work a month.
The payback period is three months.
I'm asking for approval by November first.
lessons.action: Outline one improvement idea using problem, cost, proposal, risk, ask.

options: What it costs to do nothing

lessons.title: Using AI to draft, not to think
lessons.summary: AI writes faster; you make it right.

sections.b: AI-written emails sound generic or wrong in tone.
They write the key points themselves, use AI to polish or shorten, then edit for tone, accuracy and context.
Prompt: 'Make this email shorter and more polite for a senior client; keep the numbers unchanged.' Then reread and personalise.
Sending AI drafts unread, or pasting confidential data into public tools.

speak: Please keep the numbers unchanged.
Make this shorter and more polite.
I'll review and personalise the draft.
lessons.action: Use AI to shorten one email today, then edit it in your own voice.

quiz.q: Best use of AI in writing is…
Avoid pasting into public AI tools…

lessons.title: Mapping stakeholders
lessons.summary: Know who decides, who influences and who's affected.

sections.b: Your project gets blocked by someone you didn't consult.
They list stakeholders by power and interest, and plan how to engage each.
'Before we finalise, who else should we involve? Legal and procurement may need to sign off.'
Ignoring quiet but powerful stakeholders.

speak: Who else should we involve?
Legal may need to sign off.
Let's update procurement early.
lessons.action: Draw a quick power/interest grid for your current project.

lessons.title: Influence without authority
lessons.summary: Persuade people who don't report to you.

sections.b: You need help from another team but can't order them.
They understand others' goals, offer value first, and frame requests around mutual benefit.
'I know your team wants faster approvals. If we standardise this template, both teams save time. Could we pilot it next week?'
Pulling rank, or pestering repeatedly.

speak: I know your team wants faster approvals.
This could save both teams time.
Could we pilot it next week?
lessons.action: Identify one request you need from another team and frame it around their benefit.

lessons.title: Pre-wiring decisions
lessons.summary: Discuss ideas one-on-one before big meetings.

sections.b: Your proposal gets shot down in a meeting because key people hear it for the first time.
They share ideas privately beforehand, gather feedback and address concerns, so the meeting confirms rather than debates.
'Before Thursday's meeting, could I get your view on this proposal? I'd value your input on the risks.'
Surprising senior people in big meetings.

speak: Before Thursday's meeting, could I get your view?
I'd value your input on the risks.
What would make this work for your team?
lessons.action: Before your next proposal meeting, talk to one key person privately.

options: Discussing ideas with key people before a meeting

quiz.q: Why avoid surprising seniors in meetings?
options: They may resist unfamiliar ideas publicly

lessons.title: Persuading with data and stories
lessons.summary: Numbers convince minds; stories move people.

sections.b: You present data-heavy arguments that don't persuade.
They combine one strong number with a short human story and a clear recommendation.
'Our support team spends 30% of time on password resets, about 2,000 hours a year. Last week Riya missed a client call because of it. Self-service resets would fix this.'
Data dumps without meaning, or emotional stories without data.

speak: Our team spends thirty percent of its time on password resets.
That's about two thousand hours a year.
Self-service resets would fix this.
lessons.action: Pair one key number with a short real example in your next update.

lessons.title: Building your reputation
lessons.summary: Be known for something specific.

sections.b: People don't know what you're good at beyond your job title.
They become known for a specific strength (e.g. 'the Excel automation person'), help others with it and share knowledge.

'Happy to show you the macro I built; it might save your team time too.'
Run a 15-minute lunch-and-learn.
Being invisible, or claiming expertise you don't have.

speak: Happy to show you the macro I built.
It might save your team time too.
I'm running a short session on Friday.
lessons.action: Decide what you want to be known for and share one tip about it this week.

quiz.q: A good way to build reputation is…

lessons.title: Managing expectations
lessons.summary: Under-promise and over-deliver.

sections.b: Stakeholders expect more, faster, than you can deliver.
They clarify scope, timelines and trade-offs upfront and update early when things change.
'Realistically, we can deliver the core report by Friday; the extra analysis would take another week. Which would you prefer?'
Saying yes to everything, then missing deadlines.

speak: Realistically, we can deliver the core report by Friday.
The extra analysis would take another week.
Which would you prefer?
lessons.action: For one current request, clarify scope and timeline in writing.

quiz.q: Offering a choice ('which would you prefer?')…

lessons.title: Negotiating at work
lessons.summary: Find win-win agreements on deadlines and resources.

sections.b: You accept unrealistic deadlines or fight over resources.
They understand the other side's needs, trade what's cheap for them, and use conditional offers.

'If you can share the data by Tuesday, I can deliver the forecast by Friday.'
'What's most important to you: speed or completeness?'
Accepting everything, or rigid positions.

speak: If you can share the data by Tuesday, I can deliver by Friday.
What's most important to you?
Let's find something that works for both of us.
lessons.action: Use one 'If you…, I can…' statement this week.

lessons.title: Getting buy-in for change
lessons.summary: People support what they help create.

sections.b: Your process improvement faces resistance from colleagues used to the old way.
They explain why, involve people early, address 'what's in it for me', run a small pilot and celebrate quick wins.
'This new template could save each of us an hour a week. Could we try it for two weeks and review together?'
Imposing change suddenly or dismissing concerns.

speak: This could save each of us an hour a week.
Could we try it for two weeks?
Let's review it together afterwards.
lessons.action: Propose one small improvement as a 2-week pilot with feedback.

quiz.q: People support change more when they…

lessons.title: Building alliances
lessons.summary: Allies help ideas succeed.

sections.b: You push ideas alone and run out of support.
They find people who share goals, support others' initiatives and build coalitions across teams.
'I noticed you're also working on reducing manual work. Want to combine efforts and present a joint proposal?'
Going solo on big changes, or forming cliques that exclude others.

speak: You're also working on reducing manual work.
Want to combine efforts?
We could present a joint proposal.
lessons.action: Find one colleague with a similar goal and suggest working together.

lessons.title: Earning a seat at the table
lessons.summary: Get invited to important discussions.

sections.b: Decisions affecting your work are made without you.
They add value in every interaction, ask to join relevant meetings with a clear reason, and contribute insights rather than just data.
'I'd like to join the pricing discussion. I can bring the margin analysis and highlight risks early.'
Complaining about being excluded without showing value.

speak: I'd like to join the pricing discussion.
I can bring the margin analysis.
I can highlight risks early.
lessons.action: Request to join one relevant meeting this month with a clear value statement.

lessons.title: Receiving criticism gracefully
lessons.summary: Feedback is data, not an attack.

sections.b: When someone criticises your work, you feel defensive and argue.
They listen fully, thank the person, ask clarifying questions and decide later what to act on.

'Thanks for telling me. Could you give me an example so I understand better?'
'That's helpful. I'll work on it.'
Interrupting with excuses, or taking it personally for days.

speak: Thanks for telling me.
Could you give me an example?
That's helpful, I'll work on it.
lessons.action: Next time you get feedback, say 'Thanks, can you give me an example?' before anything else.

quiz.q: First response to criticism should be…

lessons.title: Giving feedback with SBI
lessons.summary: Situation, Behaviour, Impact: specific and fair.

sections.b: You avoid giving feedback or it comes out as criticism of personality.
They describe the situation, the observable behaviour and its impact, then ask for the other person's view.
'In yesterday's client call (situation), you shared the draft numbers before they were checked (behaviour). The client is now quoting them (impact). How can we avoid that next time?'
Labels like 'You're careless', or feedback in public.

speak: In yesterday's client call, you explained the numbers very clearly.
The client felt confident as a result.
How can we avoid that next time?
lessons.action: Prepare one piece of SBI feedback (positive or constructive) and deliver it privately.

lessons.title: Delivering bad news
lessons.summary: Clear, early and with a plan.

sections.b: You must tell a client or manager about a delay or mistake.
They state the news early and clearly, explain briefly, show the plan and acknowledge impact.
'I'm afraid the report will be delayed by two days because the data had errors. We've fixed the source issue and will deliver by Thursday. I'm sorry for the inconvenience.'
Hiding the news, long excuses, or blaming others.

speak: I'm afraid the report will be delayed by two days.
We've fixed the source issue.
We'll deliver by Thursday.
lessons.action: Practise one bad-news message using: news, reason, plan, apology.

lessons.title: Saying no to your manager
lessons.summary: Protect quality by negotiating priorities.

sections.b: Your manager adds new tasks while you're already overloaded.
They don't refuse outright; they ask to re-prioritise and show trade-offs.
'I'm happy to take this on. To do it well, which of my current tasks should I pause: the audit prep or the forecast?'
Silently accepting and missing deadlines, or refusing bluntly.

speak: I'm happy to take this on.
Which current task should I pause?
I want to make sure I do it well.
lessons.action: Next time you get a new task while overloaded, ask about priorities.

quiz.q: A smart way to handle extra work is…

lessons.title: Apologising professionally
lessons.summary: A good apology repairs trust quickly.

sections.b: You made a mistake that affected others.
They apologise promptly, take responsibility, explain the fix and prevention, without over-explaining.
'I'm sorry, I sent the wrong version to the client. That's on me. I've sent the correct one and added a check before every client send.'
Blaming tools or others, or excessive apologies that make others uncomfortable.

speak: I'm sorry, that's on me.
I've sent the correct version.
I've added a check to prevent it.
lessons.action: Recall one recent mistake and write how you'd apologise using: sorry, ownership, fix, prevention.

lessons.title: Handling an angry colleague or client
lessons.summary: Lower the temperature first.

sections.b: Someone is upset and raising their voice at you.
They stay calm, let the person vent, acknowledge feelings, ask questions and move to solutions.

'I can see this is really frustrating. Let me make sure I understand what happened.'
'What would be a good outcome for you?'
Arguing back, saying 'calm down', or taking it personally.

speak: I can see this is really frustrating.
Let me make sure I understand what happened.
What would be a good outcome for you?
lessons.action: Memorise: 'I can see this is frustrating. Help me understand what happened.'

quiz.q: First step with an angry person is…

options: What would be a good outcome?

lessons.title: Performance concerns with a peer
lessons.summary: Address issues before they grow.

sections.b: A teammate's late work keeps affecting your deliverables.
They raise it privately, focus on impact, ask about obstacles and agree on next steps, escalating only if needed.
'The last two data files came after the cut-off, which delayed the report. Is something making it hard? How can we make Tuesday cut-offs work?'
Complaining to the manager first, or doing their work silently.

speak: The last two files came after the cut-off.
Is something making it hard?
How can we make the Tuesday cut-off work?
lessons.action: If a peer's delay affects you, schedule a 10-minute private chat about it.

quiz.q: Best first step with a peer's performance issue is…

lessons.title: Asking for a raise or promotion
lessons.summary: Prepare evidence, then ask clearly.

sections.b: You feel underpaid or ready for more but don't know how to ask.
They prepare achievements with numbers, market data, a clear ask, and timing (before budget cycles).

'I'd like to discuss my growth. Over the last year I automated reporting (saving 40 hours/month) and led the audit. Based on that and market data, I'd like to be considered for the senior analyst role.'
Comparing yourself to colleagues' pay, or threatening to leave.

speak: I'd like to discuss my growth.
I automated reporting and saved forty hours a month.
I'd like to be considered for the senior role.
lessons.action: List your top 3 achievements with numbers for your next growth conversation.

options: Achievements with numbers and market data

quiz.q: Good timing for such requests is…

lessons.title: Talking to your manager about a problem with them
lessons.summary: Upward feedback, carefully.

sections.b: Your manager's behaviour (last-minute changes, harsh tone) is affecting you.
They choose a private, calm moment, ask permission, use SBI and propose a solution, focusing on shared goals.
'Could I share something that would help me do better work? When requirements change on Friday evening, the team works weekends and quality drops. Could we lock changes by Thursday?'
Complaining to others, or confronting in public.

speak: Could I share something that would help me do better work?
When requirements change late, quality drops.
Could we lock changes by Thursday?
lessons.action: Write a respectful upward-feedback opener for one issue with your manager.

options: Could I share something that would help?

lessons.title: Turning feedback into action
lessons.summary: Show people you listened.

sections.b: You receive feedback but nothing visibly changes.
They choose one or two points, make a plan, act and later tell the person what changed.
'Last month you suggested shorter updates. I've switched to a 3-line format. Is that working better for you?'
Trying to fix everything at once, or forgetting feedback.

speak: Last month you suggested shorter updates.
I've switched to a three-line format.
Is that working better for you?
lessons.action: Pick one piece of feedback you received and act on it this week; then tell the person.

quiz.q: Closing the loop on feedback means…
options: Telling the person what you changed

quiz.q: How many feedback points to act on at once?

lessons.title: Understanding office politics
lessons.summary: Politics is how decisions really get made.

sections.b: You dismiss office politics as dirty and get blindsided by decisions.
They understand formal and informal power: who influences decisions, who trusts whom, and what each person wants, and they use this ethically.
Ask yourself: 'Who will be affected? Who has influence? What does each person care about?'
Ignoring politics entirely, or playing manipulative games.

speak: Who will be affected by this decision?
What does each person care about?
How can we find a solution that works for everyone?
lessons.action: Map who really influences decisions in your team (it may not be the most senior person).

options: Expertise and trust, not just title

lessons.title: Handling conflict between teammates
lessons.summary: Be a calm mediator.

sections.b: Two colleagues argue, and the team suffers.
They stay neutral, let each person explain, find common goals and agree on next steps.
'I hear two different views. Ravi, you're focused on speed; Neha, on accuracy. We both want a reliable report on time. Could we agree on a quick check step?'
Taking sides, or ignoring the conflict.

speak: I hear two different views.
We both want a reliable report on time.
Could we agree on a quick check step?
lessons.action: If you see tension in your team, summarise both sides fairly in your next discussion.

options: Stays neutral and finds common goals

quiz.q: Summarising both views helps people feel…

lessons.title: When someone takes credit for your work
lessons.summary: Reclaim credit without drama.

sections.b: A colleague presents your idea or work as theirs.
They speak up calmly in the moment or follow up privately, and make their work visible in future (emails, documents with names).

In a meeting: 'Thanks for mentioning the automation. Happy to add detail, since I built the model.'
Privately: 'I noticed my analysis was presented without mention. Next time, could we present it together?'
Public anger or silent resentment.

speak: Happy to add detail, since I built the model.
Next time, could we present it together?
I've documented the analysis in the shared folder.
lessons.action: Start documenting your contributions in shared docs and emails with your name.

lessons.title: Dealing with a micromanager
lessons.summary: Earn autonomy through trust.

sections.b: Your manager checks every detail and you feel stifled.
They over-communicate early, agree on check-in points, deliver reliably and gradually ask for more autonomy.
'To keep you updated without interrupting, could I send a short status every morning? If that works, maybe we can move to twice a week.'
Resisting openly, or hiding information (which increases micromanagement).

speak: Could I send you a short status every morning?
That way you'll always know where things stand.
Maybe later we can move to twice a week.
lessons.action: Propose a regular update rhythm to your manager.

lessons.title: Working with difficult seniors
lessons.summary: Respect hierarchy while protecting yourself.

sections.b: A senior leader is dismissive or harsh with you.
They stay professional, prepare thoroughly, keep communication concise and factual, and document key decisions.
'Understood. To make sure I get this right: you'd like the summary by 5 pm with only three key numbers?'
Reacting emotionally, or avoiding them completely.

speak: Understood.
To make sure I get this right, you'd like the summary by five?
I'll keep it to three key numbers.
lessons.action: Before your next interaction with a challenging senior, prepare your 3 key points.

quiz.q: With a harsh senior, it helps to be…

lessons.title: Navigating hierarchy in Indian workplaces
lessons.summary: Respectful but confident communication.

sections.b: Hierarchical cultures can make juniors hesitant to speak or disagree.
They show respect (titles, timing, private disagreement) while still contributing ideas confidently and with data.
'Sir/Ma'am, may I suggest an alternative? Based on last quarter's numbers, option B might reduce costs by 8%.'
Total silence, or ignoring hierarchy norms entirely.

speak: May I suggest an alternative?
Based on last quarter's numbers, option B might reduce costs.
I'd be happy to share the analysis.
lessons.action: Prepare one data-backed suggestion and share it respectfully with a senior this week.

options: Are easier for seniors to accept

lessons.title: Protecting yourself with documentation
lessons.summary: Write things down without seeming defensive.

sections.b: Verbal instructions change and you get blamed.
They confirm important verbal decisions by short email or chat and keep organised records.
'Thanks for the discussion. Just confirming: we'll go with the revised numbers and send them to the client on Monday.'
Relying on memory, or sending aggressive 'as per my last email' messages.

speak: Thanks for the discussion.
Just confirming we'll go with the revised numbers.
We'll send them to the client on Monday.
lessons.action: After your next important verbal decision, send a 2-line confirmation message.

quiz.q: 'As per my last email' can sound…

lessons.title: Staying neutral in office conflicts
lessons.summary: Don't get pulled into camps.

sections.b: Two groups or leaders are in conflict and both want your support.
They stay professional with everyone, focus on work, avoid gossip and express views on issues, not people.
'I work well with both teams. On this issue, my view is based on the data: option A meets the deadline.'
Picking sides publicly, or sharing confidential information.

speak: I work well with both teams.
My view is based on the data.
Let's focus on what helps the project.
lessons.action: If pulled into a conflict, respond with an issue-focused, neutral statement.

lessons.title: Handling unfair blame
lessons.summary: Respond with facts, not anger.

sections.b: You're blamed for a problem caused by others or by process gaps.
They stay calm, share facts and timelines, focus on the fix, and suggest process improvements.
'I understand the concern. Here's the timeline: the data reached us on the 15th, after the cut-off. To prevent this, could we set an automated reminder for data owners?'
Counter-blaming, emotional reactions or silence.

speak: I understand the concern.
Here's the timeline of what happened.
To prevent this, could we set an automated reminder?
lessons.action: Prepare a factual timeline for any current issue where blame might arise.

lessons.title: Building power ethically
lessons.summary: Earn influence through expertise and generosity.

sections.b: You feel powerless because you're not senior.
They build expertise power (being the go-to person), relationship power (wide network) and information power (knowing context), and use it to help others.

'I can help with that; I've built a similar model before.'
'Let me connect you with Priya in tax; she'll know.'
Hoarding information or using influence to harm others.

speak: I can help with that, I've built a similar model.
Let me connect you with Priya.
She'll know the answer.
lessons.action: Connect two colleagues who could help each other this week.

lessons.title: Making your work visible
lessons.summary: Good work that nobody sees doesn't count for much.

sections.b: You work hard, but leaders don't know what you've delivered.
They share short, regular updates on outcomes (not activity), credit the team and link results to business goals.
'Quick update: the new reconciliation process cut month-end close by two days. Thanks to Ravi for the automation script.'
Bragging, listing hours worked, or staying silent and hoping someone notices.

speak: Quick update on the reconciliation project.
It cut month-end close by two days.
Thanks to Ravi for the automation script.
lessons.action: Send your manager a three-line update today: what you finished, the impact, what's next.

quiz.q: Crediting the team makes you look…

lessons.title: Your 30-second introduction
lessons.summary: Introduce yourself by the value you bring.

sections.b: In meetings or events, you only say your name and job title.
They give a short line: who they are, what they help with, and something memorable or relevant to the audience.
'Hi, I'm Yash. I work in the finance analytics team; I help business units turn raw numbers into decisions. Lately I've been automating our monthly reporting.'
Long life stories, or mumbling your title and stopping.

speak: Hi, I'm Yash, from the finance analytics team.
I help business units turn numbers into decisions.
Lately I've been automating our monthly reporting.
lessons.action: Write and practise your 30-second introduction aloud three times.

quiz.q: Adding a recent project makes it…

lessons.title: Structuring a presentation
lessons.summary: Tell them the answer first, then the support.

sections.b: Your slides walk through every step before reaching the point; leaders lose interest.
They lead with the key message (the 'so what'), give three supporting points, and end with a clear ask.
'My recommendation: we move vendor payments to weekly runs. Three reasons: cash visibility, fewer errors, better discounts. I need your approval to pilot it next month.'
Data dumps, reading slides aloud, or no clear ask.

speak: My recommendation is to move to weekly payment runs.
There are three reasons.
I need your approval to pilot it next month.
lessons.action: Take your next update and rewrite the first line as the main message.

options: A clear ask or next step

lessons.title: Handling nerves when speaking
lessons.summary: Nerves are normal; preparation and breathing tame them.

sections.b: Your voice shakes and your mind goes blank when presenting.
They rehearse the opening aloud, breathe slowly before starting, pause instead of saying 'um', and focus on helping the audience.

'Let me take a moment to find that number.'
'Good question; let me think about that for a second.'
Rushing, apologising for being nervous, or memorising every word.

speak: Let me take a moment to find that number.
Good question, let me think about that.
Here's the key point.
lessons.action: Before your next meeting, take three slow breaths and practise your first sentence aloud.

lessons.title: Answering tough questions
lessons.summary: Stay calm, answer briefly, and admit what you don't know.

sections.b: A senior leader challenges your numbers in a meeting.
They listen fully, restate the question, answer in one or two sentences, and offer to follow up if unsure.

'So the question is why costs rose in Q2. The main driver was freight, up 18%. I'll send a detailed breakdown by tomorrow.'
'I don't have that figure right now; I'll confirm by 3 pm.'
Guessing, getting defensive, or giving a long rambling answer.

speak: So the question is why costs rose.
The main driver was freight.
I'll confirm that by 3 pm.
lessons.action: List three tough questions someone could ask about your current work and prepare short answers.

quiz.q: If you don't know an answer…
options: Say so and promise a follow-up

lessons.title: Executive presence
lessons.summary: How you show up: calm, clear and composed.

sections.b: You know your material, but you come across as hesitant or flustered.
They speak at a measured pace, use fewer filler words, keep good posture and eye contact, and stay calm under pressure.

'Here's where we are, here's the risk, and here's what I recommend.'
'Let's focus on what we can control.'
Upspeak (statements that sound like questions), over-apologising, or visible panic.

speak: Here's where we are.
Here's the risk.
Here's what I recommend.
lessons.action: In your next meeting, make one point slowly and finish with a firm full stop, not a question tone.

options: Focus on what they can control

lessons.title: Talking to senior leaders
lessons.summary: Short, prepared and focused on their priorities.

sections.b: You meet a senior leader in the lift or a review and freeze.
They prepare one or two talking points, connect their work to the leader's goals, and keep it short.
'Good morning. I'm on the team working on the cost-savings project. We're on track to save ₹2 crore this year.'
Complaining, oversharing details, or avoiding them completely.

speak: Good morning, I'm on the cost-savings project.
We're on track to save two crore this year.
Happy to share more if useful.
lessons.action: Prepare a two-line 'lift pitch' about your current project.

lessons.title: Building your personal brand at work
lessons.summary: Be known for something specific.

sections.b: People don't know what you're good at.
They choose one or two strengths, deliver consistently, share knowledge (short demos, notes), and help others with that skill.
'I put together a quick guide on Excel Power Query; happy to walk anyone through it.'
Trying to be known for everything, or self-promotion without substance.

speak: I put together a quick guide on Power Query.
Happy to walk anyone through it.
Let me know if it helps.
lessons.action: Pick one skill you want to be known for and share one tip about it with your team this week.

lessons.title: Networking inside the company
lessons.summary: Relationships across teams open doors.

sections.b: You only know people in your own team.
They have regular short coffee chats with people in other teams, ask about their work, and look for ways to help.
'Hi Neha, I'd love to learn more about how the treasury team works. Could we grab a 20-minute coffee this week?'
Only reaching out when you need something.

speak: I'd love to learn more about your team's work.
Could we grab a quick coffee this week?
How can I help from my side?
lessons.action: Invite one person from another team for a 20-minute chat this week.

quiz.q: A good coffee chat focuses on…
options: Their work and how to help

quiz.q: Reaching out only when you need help…

lessons.title: Asking for a promotion or raise
lessons.summary: Make a business case, not a complaint.

sections.b: You feel you deserve more but haven't asked.
They prepare evidence of impact, understand the role's expectations, ask their manager what's needed, and agree a timeline.
'I'd like to discuss my growth. Over the last year I led the close automation and mentored two analysts. What would I need to show to be considered for senior analyst?'
Comparing with colleagues' salaries, ultimatums, or asking without evidence.

speak: I'd like to discuss my growth.
Over the last year I led the close automation.
What would I need to show for the next level?
lessons.action: Start an 'impact list' today: write down three results you delivered this quarter.

quiz.q: A promotion request should be based on…
Asking 'what would I need to show?' helps…

lessons.title: Mentoring a junior
lessons.summary: Teach them to fish, patiently.

sections.b: A new joiner keeps asking you basic questions.
They make time, explain the 'why', share resources, ask questions instead of giving answers, and check in regularly.

'Good question. What do you think the first step might be?'
'Here's why we do it this way. Try it and I'll review.'
Doing the work for them, showing impatience, or making them feel stupid.

speak: Good question, what do you think?
Here's why we do it this way.
Try it and I'll review.
lessons.action: Offer a junior colleague 15 minutes this week to answer their questions.

lessons.title: Delegating well
lessons.summary: Give the outcome, context and freedom.

sections.b: You do everything yourself because it's faster.
They explain the goal, deadline and quality bar, share context, agree check-ins and let the person choose the method.
'I'd like you to own the vendor analysis. The goal is to pick the top three by Friday. Here's last year's file for context. Shall we check in Wednesday?'
Micromanaging, dumping tasks without context, or taking work back at the first problem.

speak: I'd like you to own the vendor analysis.
The goal is the top three by Friday.
Shall we check in on Wednesday?
lessons.action: Delegate one task this week using: goal, deadline, context, check-in.

lessons.title: Recognising others
lessons.summary: Specific praise motivates more than any speech.

sections.b: Your team works hard, but appreciation is rare or generic.
They praise specifically and promptly, in public when appropriate, and tell the person's manager.
'Anita, your quick reconciliation saved the client deadline. Thank you. I've let your manager know too.'
Generic 'good job', praise only at year-end, or taking the credit yourself.

speak: Your quick work saved the deadline.
Thank you, it made a real difference.
I've let your manager know too.
lessons.action: Give one colleague specific, sincere recognition today.

quiz.q: Telling someone's manager about their good work…

lessons.title: Leading without a title
lessons.summary: Influence comes from behaviour, not designation.

sections.b: You see problems but feel it's not your place to act.
They take ownership of small improvements, rally others around shared goals, and keep their manager informed.
'I noticed our handover notes are inconsistent. I've drafted a simple template; could we try it for two weeks?'
Waiting for permission for everything, or acting without informing others.

speak: I noticed our handover notes are inconsistent.
I've drafted a simple template.
Could we try it for two weeks?
lessons.action: Pick one small team problem and propose a simple fix this week.

lessons.title: Working across cultures
lessons.summary: Adapt your style to how others communicate.

sections.b: You work with colleagues from other regions and misunderstandings happen.
They learn cultural norms (directness, hierarchy, time), avoid idioms, confirm understanding in writing, and stay curious.

'Just to confirm, we agreed on Tuesday 10 am UK time for the review, correct?'
'How does your team usually prefer to receive feedback?'
Assuming everyone thinks like you, heavy slang, or stereotyping.

speak: Just to confirm, we agreed on Tuesday 10 am UK time.
How does your team prefer feedback?
Please let me know if anything was unclear.
lessons.action: Ask a colleague from another region how their team prefers to communicate.

lessons.title: Leading remote and hybrid teams
lessons.summary: Over-communicate and include everyone.

sections.b: Remote colleagues feel left out of decisions made in the office.
They document decisions, set clear norms (response times, cameras), run inclusive meetings and check in one-to-one.

'Let's hear from those online first.'
'I'll post the decision and next steps in the team channel.'
Corridor decisions, ignoring people on calls, or measuring presence instead of output.

speak: Let's hear from those online first.
I'll post the decision in the team channel.
Does anyone joining remotely have thoughts?
lessons.action: In your next hybrid meeting, invite remote participants to speak first.

quiz.q: A key habit for hybrid teams is…
Remote work is best judged by…

lessons.title: Running effective one-to-ones
lessons.summary: Their meeting, their agenda.

sections.b: Your one-to-ones turn into status updates only.
They let the other person set the agenda, ask open questions about goals and blockers, and follow up on commitments.

'What's on your mind this week?'
'What's one thing I could do to make your work easier?'
Cancelling often, talking most of the time, or only discussing tasks.

speak: What's on your mind this week?
What's getting in your way?
What could I do to make your work easier?
lessons.action: In your next one-to-one, ask 'What could I do to make your work easier?'

quiz.q: A one-to-one agenda should be led by…

lessons.title: Handling underperformance
lessons.summary: Address it early, kindly and clearly.

sections.b: A team member's work keeps slipping and you avoid the conversation.
They raise it early in private, use specific examples, listen for causes, agree clear expectations and offer support.
'I've noticed the last three reports were late. Is something getting in the way? Let's agree what on time looks like and how I can help.'
Waiting until appraisal time, public criticism, or vague hints.

speak: I've noticed the last three reports were late.
Is something getting in the way?
How can I help?
lessons.action: If someone's work is slipping, plan a private, specific conversation using SBI.

lessons.title: Building trust in a team
lessons.summary: Trust = reliability + honesty + care.

sections.b: Your team works in silos and hides problems.
They keep promises, admit their own mistakes first, share information openly and show care for people.

'I got that wrong last week; here's what I learned.'
'It's fine to raise problems early; I'd rather know.'
Punishing bad news, playing favourites, or inconsistency.

speak: I got that wrong last week.
Here's what I learned.
Please raise problems early, I'd rather know.
lessons.action: Share one mistake you made and what you learned at your next team meeting.

lessons.title: Your daily people-skills routine
lessons.summary: Small daily habits compound into a reputation.

sections.b: You've learned many skills, but you need to practise them every day.
They follow a simple routine: greet people by name, listen fully in one conversation, send one clear update, give one specific thank-you, and reflect for two minutes at day's end.

Morning: 'Good morning, Priya! How was your weekend?'
Day: 'Quick update: the draft is ready for review.'
Evening: 'Thanks, Ravi, your help today made a difference.'
Trying to change everything at once, or giving up after one bad day.

speak: Good morning, how was your weekend?
Quick update, the draft is ready for review.
Thanks, your help today made a difference.
lessons.action: Start the routine today and write a two-line reflection tonight: what went well, what to try tomorrow.

options: What went well and what to try next

quiz.q: After a bad day, you should…
